```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5)
```

This guide shows how to fit the models of the accompanying paper to a series
of N-of-1 trials, how to read the output, and how to reproduce the analysis
of the Raynaud data in the paper. The samplers in this package are the code
that produced every result in the paper.

# The models

Let $y_{ik}$ be the $k$-th outcome of patient $i = 1, \dots, N$. All models use
$$
y_{ik} = \mu_i + \beta_i A_{ik} + \alpha t_{ik} + \mathbf{B}_{ik}^\top \boldsymbol\gamma + \delta P_{ik} + \varepsilon_{ik},
$$
where $A_{ik}$ indicates active treatment, $t_{ik}$ is the day within the
treatment period, $\mathbf{B}_{ik}$ holds block indicators and $P_{ik}$
indicates the second period within a block. The patient-specific treatment
effect $\beta_i$ is the parameter of interest. The time, block and period
effects have spike-and-slab priors, and the errors are either independent or
AR(1) within each treatment period. The models differ in the prior on the
$\mu_i$ and $\beta_i$:

* **Hierarchical model** (`hierarchical_sampler()`): $\beta_i \sim N(\tilde\beta, \sigma^2_\beta)$
  with a half-Cauchy prior on $\sigma_\beta$. Every patient borrows from the
  same population distribution.
* **Home--host clustering model** (`clustering_sampler()`): each patient is either a
  *home* with its own value $b_i \sim N(m, \tau^2)$, or a *guest* that takes
  the value of a home. The prior on the indicators is
  $p(\boldsymbol\zeta) \propto r^{N-K}$ with $r = p_c/(1-p_c)$, where $K$ is
  the number of homes (clusters) and $p_c$ is the clustering probability.
  Patients borrow exactly within a cluster and partially across clusters.
  As $p_c \to 0$ every patient is its own home and the model becomes the
  hierarchical model.
* **No-pooling reference**: the hierarchical model with the between-patient
  variances fixed at 25 (`hierarchical_sampler(..., sigma_sq_mu = 25, sigma_sq_beta = 25)`),
  so that each $\beta_i$ is estimated almost entirely from the patient's own data.

# Data format

```{r data}
library(BayesClustNof1)
head(nof1_example)
```

Each sampler takes the columns as separate vectors:

| Argument | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `ID` | patient identifier |
| `Y`  | outcome |
| `A`  | treatment (the lowest value is the control condition) |
| `t`  | day within the treatment period |
| `B`  | block (the lowest value is the reference block) |
| `P`  | position of the period within its block (the lowest value is the reference) |

The data must be **sorted by patient and time**, because the AR(1) errors
restart at the start of every treatment period and are evaluated in that
order. `nof1_example` has 10 patients, 5 blocks and 6 days per period.
Patients 3 and 7 respond to treatment (true effect 1.5); the others do not.

# Fitting the models

`iter` is the total number of iterations; the first half is discarded as
burn-in. The paper uses 20,000 iterations and `ar1 = TRUE`.

```{r fit}
d <- nof1_example
set.seed(1)
fit_c <- clustering_sampler(iter = 20000, ID = d$ID, Y = d$Y, A = d$A, t = d$t,
                            B = d$B, P = d$P, clust_prob = 0.3, ar1 = TRUE)
set.seed(1)
fit_h <- hierarchical_sampler(iter = 20000, ID = d$ID, Y = d$Y, A = d$A, t = d$t,
                              B = d$B, P = d$P, ar1 = TRUE)
```

# Patient-specific treatment effects

`subject_summary` gives the posterior mean and 95% credible interval of each
$\mu_i$ and $\beta_i$. The posterior draws after burn-in are in
`posterior_samples`; from them we compute the posterior probability of
benefit, $P(\beta_i > 0 \mid y)$.

```{r effects}
p_benefit <- function(fit) colMeans(fit$posterior_samples$beta > 0)
truth <- tapply(d$beta_true, d$ID, unique)
data.frame(ID = fit_c$subject_summary$ID, true = truth,
           clustering = round(fit_c$subject_summary$beta, 2),
           clustering_95CI = fit_c$subject_summary$beta_95CI,
           P_benefit_clust = round(p_benefit(fit_c), 3),
           hierarchical = round(fit_h$subject_summary$beta, 2),
           P_benefit_hier = round(p_benefit(fit_h), 3))
```

In the paper a patient is called a responder when $P(\beta_i > 0 \mid y) > 0.95$:

```{r responders}
which(p_benefit(fit_c) > 0.95)
which(p_benefit(fit_h) > 0.95)
```

A forest plot of the two fits:

```{r forest, fig.height = 5}
ci <- function(fit) apply(fit$posterior_samples$beta, 2, quantile, c(0.025, 0.975))
N <- length(truth); yy <- seq_len(N)
plot(NA, xlim = range(ci(fit_c), ci(fit_h)), ylim = c(0.5, N + 0.5), yaxt = "n",
     xlab = expression(beta[i]), ylab = "Patient")
axis(2, at = yy, labels = names(truth), las = 1); abline(v = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
segments(ci(fit_c)[1, ], yy + 0.15, ci(fit_c)[2, ], yy + 0.15, col = "#1b6ca8", lwd = 2)
points(fit_c$subject_summary$beta, yy + 0.15, pch = 19, col = "#1b6ca8")
segments(ci(fit_h)[1, ], yy - 0.15, ci(fit_h)[2, ], yy - 0.15, col = "#c0392b", lwd = 2)
points(fit_h$subject_summary$beta, yy - 0.15, pch = 17, col = "#c0392b")
points(truth, yy, pch = 4, cex = 1.2)
legend("bottomright", c("Clustering", "Hierarchical", "True effect"), pch = c(19, 17, 4),
       col = c("#1b6ca8", "#c0392b", "black"), bty = "n")
```

# Other parameters

```{r other}
fit_c$other_summary      # error variance, base mean and SD, rho
fit_c$alpha_summary      # time effect and its inclusion probability
fit_c$gamma_summary      # block effects
fit_c$delta_summary      # period effect
```

`RaoBlackwell_Pr` is the posterior inclusion probability of each nuisance
effect, averaged over the conditional probabilities (lower Monte Carlo error
than the proportion of draws).

# Clusters and similarity between patients

`coclustering_beta[i, j]` is the posterior probability that patients $i$ and
$j$ share the same treatment effect.

```{r cocluster, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5}
S <- fit_c$coclustering_beta
image(1:N, 1:N, S[, N:1], zlim = c(0, 1), axes = FALSE, xlab = "Patient", ylab = "Patient",
      col = hcl.colors(20, "Blues 3", rev = TRUE))
axis(1, 1:N); axis(2, 1:N, labels = N:1, las = 1)
round(S[c(3, 7), ], 2)
```

The posterior number of clusters, and a single partition that summarises the
posterior (minimising the expected variation of information):

```{r partition}
fit_c$n_clusters_summary
part <- estimate_partition(fit_c$posterior_samples$zeta_beta, loss = "VI")
part
```

# Choosing the clustering probability

$p_c$ sets the prior number of clusters. For $N = 10$ the prior mean of $K$
is 6.9, 5.4, 4.5 and 3.0 for $p_c = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.9$. The paper uses
$p_c = 0.3$ and reports how the results depend on $p_c$. It is good practice
to refit the model with several values:

```{r sensitivity}
sens <- sapply(c(0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.9), function(pc) {
  set.seed(1)
  f <- clustering_sampler(20000, d$ID, d$Y, d$A, d$t, d$B, d$P, clust_prob = pc, ar1 = TRUE)
  c(p_c = pc, RMSE = sqrt(mean((f$subject_summary$beta - truth)^2)),
    mean_K = f$n_clusters_summary$mean[2])
})
round(t(sens), 3)
```

(The RMSE uses the known true effects, so it is only available for simulated data.)

# Checking convergence

Run several chains from different seeds and compare them, for example with
the potential scale reduction factor of each $\beta_i$:

```{r convergence}
chains <- lapply(1:3, function(s) {
  set.seed(100 + s)
  clustering_sampler(20000, d$ID, d$Y, d$A, d$t, d$B, d$P, clust_prob = 0.3, ar1 = TRUE)$posterior_samples$beta
})
rhat <- function(x) {                           # x: draws x chains
  n <- nrow(x); B <- n * var(colMeans(x)); W <- mean(apply(x, 2, var))
  sqrt(((n - 1) / n * W + B / n) / W)
}
round(sapply(1:N, function(i) rhat(sapply(chains, function(ch) ch[, i]))), 3)
plot(chains[[1]][, 3], type = "l", col = "grey40", xlab = "Iteration after burn-in",
     ylab = expression(beta[3]))
```

# Further options

* `ar1 = FALSE` assumes independent errors.
* `hierarchical_sampler(..., sigma_sq_mu = 25, sigma_sq_beta = 25)` gives the
  no-pooling reference used in the paper.
* `A_beta`, `A_tau_beta` (and `A_mu`, `A_tau_mu`) set the half-Cauchy scales,
  in the units of the outcome; the defaults are 1 for the treatment effects and
  5 for the patient means.
* `p_zeta_alpha`, `p_zeta_gamma`, `p_zeta_delta` and `sigma_sq_alpha`,
  `sigma_sq_gamma`, `sigma_sq_delta` set the spike-and-slab priors
  (defaults 0.1 and 1).
* `fit$raw` holds every draw, including the burn-in.

# Reproducing the Raynaud analysis in the paper

The paper reanalyses the series of N-of-1 trials of sildenafil for Raynaud
phenomenon (Roustit et al., 2018), comparing placebo with sildenafil 40 mg in
38 patients (1,537 daily observations). These data are included as `raynaud`
(see `?raynaud` for how they were derived from the public data). Lower scores
mean fewer symptoms, so $\beta_i < 0$ favours sildenafil.

The paper fits the hierarchical model, the clustering model with $p_c = 0.3$
and the no-pooling reference, each with independent and with AR(1) errors,
using 20,000 iterations and seed 123. The following code refits all six
models (about a minute) and rebuilds the table of the application in the
paper; the posterior draws are identical to those reported.

```{r raynaud-fit}
r <- raynaud
fit_raynaud <- function(model, ar1) {
  set.seed(123)
  switch(model,
    hier   = hierarchical_sampler(20000, r$ID, r$Y, r$A, r$t, r$B, r$P, ar1 = ar1),
    clust  = clustering_sampler(20000, r$ID, r$Y, r$A, r$t, r$B, r$P, clust_prob = 0.3, ar1 = ar1),
    nopool = hierarchical_sampler(20000, r$ID, r$Y, r$A, r$t, r$B, r$P,
                                  sigma_sq_mu = 25, sigma_sq_beta = 25, ar1 = ar1))
}
ray <- list()
for (ar1 in c(FALSE, TRUE)) for (m in c("hier", "clust", "nopool"))
  ray[[paste0(m, if (ar1) "_AR1" else "")]] <- fit_raynaud(m, ar1)
```

```{r raynaud-table}
ids <- ray$hier$subject_summary$ID
f2 <- function(x) sub("^-(0\\.0+)$", "\\1", sprintf("%.2f", x))     # print -0.00 as 0.00
est <- function(x) sprintf("%s (%s, %s)", f2(mean(x)), f2(quantile(x, 0.025)), f2(quantile(x, 0.975)))
width <- function(f) mean(apply(f$posterior_samples$beta, 2, function(x) diff(quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975)))))
n95 <- function(f) sum(apply(f$posterior_samples$beta, 2, function(x) {
  q <- quantile(x, c(0.025, 0.975)); q[1] > 0 | q[2] < 0 }))
K <- function(f) if (is.null(f$posterior_samples$zeta_beta)) "--" else
  sprintf("%.1f", mean(apply(f$posterior_samples$zeta_beta, 1, function(z) length(unique(z)))))
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(ray), function(nm) {
  f <- ray[[nm]]; B <- f$posterior_samples$beta
  data.frame(errors = if (grepl("AR1", nm)) "AR(1)" else "independent",
             model = c(hier = "Hierarchical", clust = "Clustering (p_c = 0.3)",
                       nopool = "No pooling")[sub("_AR1", "", nm)],
             beta_bar = est(f$beta_bar),
             beta_31 = est(B[, ids == 31]), beta_32 = est(B[, ids == 32]),
             width = f2(width(f)), n95 = n95(f),
             rho = if (grepl("AR1", nm)) f2(mean(f$posterior_samples$rho)) else "--",
             K_beta = K(f))
}))
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

Here $\bar\beta$ is the average of the 38 patient effects, $\beta_{31}$ and
$\beta_{32}$ are the patients with the most negative and most positive
separate estimates, width is the mean width of the 95% intervals of the
$\beta_i$, $n_{95}$ is the number of patients whose 95% interval excludes zero,
and $K_\beta$ is the posterior mean number of clusters.

The posterior probability that each patient benefits, $P(\beta_i < 0 \mid y)$,
in the models with AR(1) errors:

```{r raynaud-benefit}
p_sild <- function(f) colMeans(f$posterior_samples$beta < 0)
round(sapply(ray[c("hier_AR1", "clust_AR1", "nopool_AR1")], function(f) range(p_sild(f))), 2)
```

The models that pool find little heterogeneity and no individual responder;
the no-pooling reference gives much wider intervals.

# Reference

Roustit M, Giai J, Gaget O, et al. (2018). On-demand sildenafil as a treatment
for Raynaud phenomenon: a series of n-of-1 trials. *Annals of Internal
Medicine*, 169, 694--703.
